entries.label: Right letters, wrong order around the shape
entries.description: The student checks that a shape's corners carry the correct alphabet letters (e.g. A, B, C, D) and stops there, without tracing the perimeter to confirm the letters actually run in alphabetical order, clockwise or anticlockwise, from one corner to the next.

refutation.text_md: You've checked that the shape's corners are labeled with the letters A, B, C and D — that's the right set of letters, so part of the check is already done.

But having the right letters isn't the same as having them in the right order. In each of these questions, all four drawings are the exact same shape — they only differ in which corner gets which letter — and only one of the four arrangements has the letters running A, B, C, D as you trace around the outside, either clockwise or anticlockwise. The book rules out the other three even though every one of them uses the same four letters.

So the letters can jump around the shape — say from A straight across to C, skipping B — and still look alphabetical at a glance, while failing the convention, because reading them off corner by corner around the perimeter doesn't give a straight run of the alphabet.

Check it by tracing: start at any corner, follow the edges all the way round in one direction, and read off the letters as you pass each corner. If they come out as a straight run — A, B, C, D, or that same run read backwards — the naming is correct; if any letter is out of step, it isn't, no matter which letters were used.

entries.label: Used the wrong point's coordinates for one distance
entries.description: The student computes one of several pairwise distances using another point's coordinates by mistake — most often when two of the labelled points share a coordinate — so that distance comes out matching a distance already found, making sides look equal when they are not.

refutation.text_md: You found $QR=5$ and $PR=5$ correctly, so the distance formula itself isn't the problem. For $PQ$ it looks like $R$'s coordinates slipped in instead of $Q$'s — an easy mix-up here, since $Q(1, 3)$ and $R(1, -2)$ share the same $x$-value of $1$.

The book's rule for $PQ$ uses only $P(5, 1)$ and $Q(1, 3)$: $PQ=\sqrt{(5-1)^{2}+(1-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}$. That is not $5$ — it's a different value in surd form — so $PQ$ does not match $QR$ or $PR$.
Only two sides match ($QR=PR=5$), and $PQ=2\sqrt{5}$ is different, so $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles, not equilateral. All three sides equal would need $PQ$ to also come out as $5$, and it doesn't.

Before each distance, write down exactly which two labelled points you're using right next to the formula — e.g. $PQ:\ P(5, 1)\ \text{and}\ Q(1, 3)$ — so when two points share a coordinate like $Q$ and $R$ do here, the right point stays attached to the right label.

entries.label: Turned subtracting a negative coordinate into an ordinary subtraction
entries.description: When a coordinate is negative, the student computes the difference as if the minus signs cancelled out only once, e.g. taking $y_1-(-2)$ as $y_1-2$ instead of $y_1+2$, so any side built from that point comes out too short.

refutation.text_md: You're using the right tool — the distance formula on all three sides — which is exactly the correct plan for classifying $\triangle PQR$. The slip shows up wherever a coordinate is negative: at $R(1, -2)$, subtracting $-2$ seems to have been read as subtracting $2$.

Look at $QR$: from $Q(1, 3)$ to $R(1, -2)$ you need $y_{1}-y_{2}=3-(-2)$. The book keeps both minus signs and gets $3+2=5$, so $d_{QR}=\sqrt{0^{2}+5^{2}}=5$. Dropping the second negative instead gives $3-2=1$, shrinking $d_{QR}$ to $\sqrt{0^{2}+1^{2}}=1$ — a completely different, much smaller side.

The same slip happens again on $PR$, since $P(5, 1)$ to $R(1, -2)$ also subtracts $R$'s $-2$. Once both of those sides come out too short, $QR$ and $PR$ no longer match each other or $PQ$, and the triangle looks scalene when it is really isosceles, with $QR=PR=5$.

Whenever a coordinate is negative, write the subtraction out with its bracket first — $3-(-2)$ — before simplifying, and turn the two minus signs into a plus: $3+2$. Do that for every negative coordinate and the matching sides show up correctly.

entries.label: Drops the second root
entries.description: After squaring and simplifying to something like $(\text{expr})^{2}=\text{number}$, the student takes only the positive square root and states a single value, missing that the other sign also solves the equation and gives a second valid point.
entries.signal: Final answer states only one value where the canonical answer has two (e.g. gives $y=-3$ alone instead of $y=-3$ or $y=21$), with no second value joined by "or".

refutation.text_md: You're solving correctly, and squaring is the right move — you're just stopping one step too early. Once you reach something like $(9-y)^{2}=144$, taking the positive square root and writing $9-y=12$ (so $y=-3$) is a completely reasonable instinct, since a distance is positive.

But $(9-y)^{2}=144$ is also true when $9-y=-12$. In the worked example, $R(3,9)$ and $S(8,y)$ with $RS=13$, solving gives $y=-3$ or $y=21$ — and checking both back in the distance formula gives the same result: $y=-3$ gives $d=\sqrt{25+144}=13$, and $y=21$ gives $d=\sqrt{25+144}=13$ too. Both points really are 13 units from $R$; dropping $y=21$ throws away a real answer, not a wrong one.
This happens every time here because the distance formula squares the coordinate difference, so an equation like $(y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}=\text{number}$ has two solutions unless that number is $0$.

So once you reach $(\text{something})^{2}=\text{number}$, write both $+\sqrt{\text{number}}$ and $-\sqrt{\text{number}}$, solve for both values, and only then check the question to see whether it wants one of them or both.

entries.label: Keeps both roots without filtering
entries.description: The student correctly solves the quadratic and gets two values that both satisfy the distance equation, but reports both as the final answer even when the question's picture or a stated condition (such as $k\geq0$) means only one of them is the point actually being asked about.
entries.signal: Final answer lists both values joined by "or" where the canonical answer keeps only one (e.g. gives $x=1$ or $x=-3$ instead of $x=1$).

refutation.text_md: You did the algebra right — solving the quadratic and getting two numbers that both satisfy the distance equation is exactly the correct work, and it's natural to give both as "the answer" since both genuinely check out.

But some of this objective's questions ask for the coordinate of one specific point that's already drawn or already constrained, so only one of your two values is actually that point. Take the quadrilateral question: $C(0,-5)$ and $D(4,k)$ with $CD=\sqrt{52}$ and $k\geq0$. Solving gives $k=1$ or $k=-11$, and both really do satisfy $\sqrt{16+(k+5)^{2}}=\sqrt{52}$. But the question also states $k\geq0$, so $k=-11$ is thrown out — not because the algebra is wrong, but because it fails the condition you were given.

The picture questions work the same way: both numbers solve the distance equation, but only one matches where the point is actually shown on the grid — the other solves for a mirror-image point that isn't the one in the picture.

So after you solve the quadratic, go back to the question: is there a range given (like $k\geq0$), or a picture showing where the point sits? Use that to pick. If the question gives no such extra condition — as in most of this objective's other questions — both values are correct and you keep both.

entries.label: Different point order on top and bottom of the formula
entries.description: The student substitutes the two points in one order for the numerator (e.g. $y_1-y_2$) but keeps the opposite order for the denominator (e.g. $x_2-x_1$), which flips the sign of the gradient.
entries.signal: The student's numeric answer is the exact negative of the canonical gradient (same magnitude, opposite sign).

refutation.text_md: You've swapped the order on the top of the fraction but kept the same order on the bottom — for instance writing $y_1-y_2$ over $x_2-x_1$. Your formula and your numbers are otherwise right; only the labelling order doesn't match between numerator and denominator.

That mismatch flips the sign of the answer. Take $E(2,5)$ and $F(-3,9)$ from the worked example: keeping the same order in both gives $m_{EF}=\frac{9-5}{-3-2}=\frac{4}{-5}=-\frac{4}{5}$. Swap only the top to $\frac{5-9}{-3-2}$ and you get $\frac{-4}{-5}=\frac{4}{5}$ — the opposite sign from the book's $-\frac{4}{5}$.
Pick which point is point 1 and which is point 2 once, then keep that same order in both the top and the bottom: $m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.

entries.label: Uses the segment's original points instead of the ones the question asks about
entries.description: When the two points needed are constructed from others (e.g. as mid-points of two given segments), the student substitutes the coordinates of the original named points into the gradient formula instead of first finding the constructed points the question actually asks about.

refutation.text_md: It's tempting to reach for the coordinates of the points already named in the question — here $Q$ and $R$ — rather than first working out the pair of points the question is actually asking about. You'd get a correctly-computed gradient this way — just for the wrong segment.

For $P(5,1)$, $Q(1,3)$, $R(1,-2)$, using $Q$ and $R$ directly gives $m_{QR}=\frac{-2-3}{1-1}=\frac{-5}{0}$, which is undefined because $Q$ and $R$ share the same $x$-coordinate. But the question asks for the gradient of $ST$, where $S$ is the mid-point of $PQ$ and $T$ is the mid-point of $QR$: $S(3,2)$ and $T(1,0.5)$, giving $m_{ST}=\frac{2-0.5}{3-1}=\frac{1.5}{2}=\frac{3}{4}$.

Before substituting into the gradient formula, first work out the actual two points the question names — here the mid-points $S$ and $T$ — and only then put those coordinates into $m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.

entries.label: Gradient formula written upside down
entries.description: The student writes the gradient formula with the $x$-difference on top and the $y$-difference on the bottom, $\frac{x_2-x_1}{y_2-y_1}$, instead of the book's $\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$, and solves the rearranged equation with the fraction that way round.
entries.signal: The final answer equals what solving the book's formula would give using $\frac{1}{m}$ (the reciprocal of the stated gradient) in place of $m$.

refutation.text_md: You set up two coordinate differences, one for $x$ and one for $y$ — that part is right. But you put the $x$-difference on top and the $y$-difference on the bottom, the opposite way round from the book's $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.
Try it on $G(7, -9)$ and $H(x, 0)$ with $m_{GH}=3$: written that way round you'd get $3=\dfrac{x-7}{0-(-9)}=\dfrac{x-7}{9}$, so $x-7=27$ and $x=34$.
But the book keeps the $y$-difference on top: $3=\dfrac{0-(-9)}{x-7}=\dfrac{9}{x-7}$, so $x-7=3$ and $x=10$ — the answer in the worked solution, not $34$.

Writing the fraction upside down is, every time, the same as solving with $\frac{1}{m}$ instead of $m$. So before substituting, write $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$ out first, check a $y$-difference sits on top and an $x$-difference sits on the bottom, then fill in the numbers from the question.

entries.label: Point order mismatched between top and bottom
entries.description: The student uses a different point as 'first' in the $x$-difference than in the $y$-difference (for example $y_2-y_1$ over $x_1-x_2$ instead of over $x_2-x_1$), which silently flips the sign of the equation being solved.
entries.signal: The final answer equals what solving the book's formula would give using $-m$ in place of the stated gradient $m$.

refutation.text_md: You set up an $x$-difference and a $y$-difference — the right shape for the formula. But you didn't keep the same point first in both: for example you used $y_2-y_1$ on top but $x_1-x_2$ on the bottom, instead of $x_2-x_1$.
Try it on $G(7,-9)$ and $H(x,0)$ with $m_{GH}=3$: keeping $H$ first only in the denominator gives $3=\dfrac{0-(-9)}{7-x}=\dfrac{9}{7-x}$, so $7-x=3$ and $x=4$.

The book keeps $H$ first in both places: $3=\dfrac{0-(-9)}{x-7}=\dfrac{9}{x-7}$, so $x=10$ — not $4$. Swapping the order in just one of the two differences flips its sign, so the equation ends up solved as though the gradient were $-3$ instead of $3$.

Choose which point is $(x_1, y_1)$ and which is $(x_2, y_2)$ once, at the start, and reuse that same choice for both differences — never let a different point come first in the $x$-difference than in the $y$-difference.

entries.label: Judges parallel sides by the sketch, not the gradients
entries.description: Decides which sides of a quadrilateral are parallel — and so what kind of quadrilateral it is — from how the figure looks, or from checking only one pair of sides, instead of calculating and comparing the gradient of every pair of opposite sides.

refutation.text_md: You're going by the shape as drawn — for $FGHI$ that doesn't look like a tidy parallelogram, and for $PQRS$ you may have felt it matched, or half-matched, a familiar shape. That instinct about symmetry is a reasonable first guess.

But the book settles this by calculating every side's gradient, not by the picture. For $F(2, 0)$, $G(1, 5)$, $H(3, 7)$, $I(7, 2)$: $m_{FG}=-5$, $m_{HI}=-\dfrac{5}{4}$, $m_{GH}=1$, $m_{FI}=\dfrac{2}{5}$ — none of the opposite pairs match, so $FGHI$ is an ordinary quadrilateral however it looks.

The same check applies to $PQRS$: the book's own answer there is trapezium — exactly one pair of the four sides has matching gradients, not both pairs (which would make it a parallelogram) and not neither pair (which would make it an ordinary quadrilateral).
So work out the gradient of all four sides before naming the shape, and let the exact numbers — not the sketch, and not just the first pair you tried — tell you which sides are parallel.

entries.label: Forces a value for $k$ the algebra rules out
entries.description: Pushes the parallel-gradient algebra through to a specific number for $k$ instead of recognising that the equation has no solution because the two lines already share the given point.
entries.signal: gives any specific numeric value for $k$ in this question, instead of stating that no value of $k$ works.

refutation.text_md: You set up exactly the right idea — for $AD$ to be parallel to $CD$ you need $m_{AD}=m_{CD}$ — and pushing the algebra through to a number is exactly the instinct that works on every other question like this one.

But look at what the algebra actually gives here: $\dfrac{k-5}{4}=\dfrac{k+5}{4}$ leads to $k-5=k+5$, which simplifies to $0=10$ — a statement that's never true, whatever $k$ is. That's different from every other 'find the missing coordinate' question in this set, where the same steps land on one clean value.

The reason is in the points themselves: $D$ is the one point that both $AD$ and $CD$ pass through. Two different lines through the same point can only be parallel if they're actually the same line, and $A(0, 5)$, $C(0, -5)$, $D(4, k)$ can never all sit on one line — so $AD$ and $CD$ can never be parallel, whatever $k$ is.
So whenever the gradient equation collapses to something like $0=10$, that's the answer: no value works — don't keep solving for a number that isn't there.

entries.label: Wrong test for 'perpendicular'
entries.description: Judges two lines 'perpendicular' from a rough stand-in — the gradients being equal, or merely opposite in sign — instead of checking that their product is exactly $-1$.
entries.signal: answers 'perpendicular' for a pair of lines whose gradients are equal, or merely opposite in sign, while their actual product is not $-1$.

refutation.text_md: You've got two real clues for perpendicular lines in mind — equal gradients feeling like a strong match, or gradients pointing opposite ways feeling like the lines cross squarely — so reaching for one of those isn't a strange thing to try.

But the book's test is neither of those: it's that $m_{AB}\times m_{CD}=-1$ exactly — the gradients are the negative inverses of each other. Take $A(3, -4)$, $B(5, 2)$, $C(-1, -1)$, $D(7, 23)$: $m_{AB}=3$ and $m_{CD}=3$ — equal — but $3\times3=9$, not $-1$, so these lines are parallel, not perpendicular, even though the gradients match exactly.

Take $A(3, -4)$, $B(5, 2)$, $C(-1, -1)$, $D(0, -4)$ instead: $m_{AB}=3$ and $m_{CD}=-3$ — opposite signs — but $3\times(-3)=-9$, not $-1$, so this pair isn't perpendicular either; they're neither parallel nor perpendicular.
So always multiply the two gradients together and check the product against $-1$ itself — equal gradients or opposite signs are not a substitute for that one calculation.

entries.label: Swaps point order between rise and run
entries.description: Computes the rise and the run for one gradient by taking the two points in different orders (e.g. $y_1-y_2$ over $x_2-x_1$), which flips that gradient's sign and throws off the comparison with the other line.

refutation.text_md: You're using the right formula, $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$ — the slip is only in which point you call '1' and which you call '2' when you move from the top of the fraction to the bottom.

Look at $C(-1, -1)$ and $D(0, -4)$: the book always takes both the $y$'s and the $x$'s in the same order, $D$ then $C$: $m_{CD}=\dfrac{-4-(-1)}{0-(-1)}=\dfrac{-3}{1}=-3$. Take the $y$'s as $C$ then $D$ while leaving the $x$'s as $D$ then $C$, and you get $\dfrac{-1-(-4)}{0-(-1)}=\dfrac{3}{1}=3$ instead — the sign flips, and a line that really isn't parallel to $AB$ ($m_{AB}=3$, true $m_{CD}=-3$) suddenly looks like it matches.

The same slip explains the other wrong pick, just the other way round. For $A(3, -4)$, $B(5, 2)$, $C(-1, -1)$, $D(7, 23)$ the book gets $m_{AB}=3$ and $m_{CD}=3$ — genuinely parallel. Mismatch the order on $CD$ the same way — $y$'s as $C$ then $D$, $x$'s as $D$ then $C$ — and you get $\dfrac{-1-23}{7-(-1)}=\dfrac{-24}{8}=-3$. Now $3$ and $-3$ are neither equal nor negative inverses of each other, so a genuinely parallel pair ends up looking like neither.
So once you decide which point is '1' and which is '2' for a gradient, keep that same choice for both the $y$'s on top and the $x$'s on the bottom — then compare the two finished numbers.

entries.label: Equal gradient read as parallel, not the same line
entries.description: The student computes both segment gradients correctly, finds them equal, but concludes the points are NOT collinear — reading the matching gradient as 'these two segments are parallel' instead of noticing the segments share a point and so must be one line.
entries.signal: Final answer is 'not collinear' even though the two computed segment gradients are equal.

refutation.text_md: You got both gradients right — $m_{EF}=-1$ and $m_{FG}=-1$ — and you saw they matched. But then you read 'equal gradient' as 'parallel lines', and since parallel lines never meet, you answered not collinear.

Parallel lines are two different lines running side by side that never touch. That is not the situation here: $EF$ and $FG$ are not two separate tracks — they share the actual point $F$. A line through $F$ with gradient $-1$ is one line, so a segment leaving $F$ with that same gradient $-1$ has to be lying along that same line, not running parallel next to it.
Check it against $H(-3, -5)$, $I(0, 0)$, $J(6, 10)$ too: $m_{HI}=m_{IJ}=\frac{5}{3}$, sharing the point $I$ — same reasoning, same answer: collinear.
So keep this rule: two segments that share a point and have the same gradient are one line, not two parallel ones — that shared point is exactly what turns 'equal gradient' into 'collinear'.

entries.label: Same-sign gradients assumed equal
entries.description: The student computes both segment gradients correctly but, seeing that both are negative, treats them as matching without checking the actual fraction values, and concludes the points ARE collinear.
entries.signal: Final answer is 'collinear' even though the two computed segment gradients are unequal fractions that merely share the same sign.

refutation.text_md: You worked out both gradients right — $m_{KL}=-\frac{1}{3}$ and $m_{LM}=-\frac{1}{2}$ — and since both are negative, they looked like the same tilt, so you answered collinear.
Both negative only tells you both segments slope downward from left to right — it doesn't tell you they slope down by the same amount. $\frac{1}{3}$ is not $\frac{1}{2}$, so $m_{KL}\neq m_{LM}$.

Because the gradients differ, the path from $K$ to $L$ doesn't carry straight on once it reaches $L$ — it bends before it gets to $M$. That's exactly why $K(-6, 2)$, $L(-3, 1)$ and $M(1, -1)$ are not collinear.
So don't stop at matching signs — compare the actual fraction. Two gradients only mean one line when they're the same value, sign included, not just the same sign.

entries.label: Assuming any quadrilateral's diagonals bisect each other
entries.description: The student answers that a shape's diagonals bisect each other on sight (or because it looks like a parallelogram), instead of finding the mid-point of each diagonal with the mid-point formula and comparing them.
entries.signal: answers 'bisect' (or claims the mid-points match) without showing the mid-point of each diagonal worked out and compared separately

refutation.text_md: You know that in shapes like parallelograms the diagonals cross exactly at their shared mid-point — that's a good instinct. The slip is expecting that for every four-sided shape, without actually checking it.
The book's own method checks it directly: find the mid-point of each diagonal with the mid-point formula, then see whether the two mid-points are the same point.

For $FGHI$ with $F(2, 0)$, $G(1, 5)$, $H(3, 7)$, $I(7, 2)$: $M_{GI}=\left(\frac{1+7}{2}, \frac{5+2}{2}\right)=\left(4, \frac{7}{2}\right)$, while $M_{FH}=\left(\frac{3+2}{2}, \frac{7+0}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{5}{2}, \frac{7}{2}\right)$.
$M_{GI}\ne M_{FH}$, so here the diagonals do not bisect each other — and that's the check to run every time: calculate both mid-points with the formula and compare them before answering.

entries.label: Dropping a sign when a coordinate is negative
entries.description: When an endpoint has a negative coordinate, the student loses or mishandles the minus sign while adding $x_1+x_2$ or $y_1+y_2$ in the mid-point formula, so the mid-point comes out with the wrong sign.
entries.signal: the computed mid-point has a flipped sign on the $x$- or $y$-coordinate compared to the canonical answer, often landing it on the wrong side of an axis from what a quick sketch would suggest

refutation.text_md: You added the coordinates the right way round, but a minus sign got lost along the way — easy to do when one of the points already has a negative coordinate.
Worked Example 10 sketches this out first: for $E(2, 1)$ and $G(-2, -2)$, the sketch already tells us the mid-point $F$ should have a negative $y$-coordinate.

If the sign on $y_2=-2$ gets lost, $y=\frac{y_1+y_2}{2}$ turns into $\frac{1+2}{2}=\frac{3}{2}$ instead of $\frac{1+(-2)}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}$ — positive, where the sketch already said it should be negative.

Keep each coordinate's own sign inside the brackets before adding — write $\frac{1+(-2)}{2}$, not $\frac{1+2}{2}$ — and then check the sign of your answer against a quick sketch, the way the book does right after Worked Example 11.

entries.label: Forgot to double the mid-point
entries.description: Sets up the mid-point equation correctly but solves it as if the mid-point already equalled the sum of the two end points, skipping the step that multiplies both sides by 2, so the unknown end point comes out as (known point subtracted from the mid-point) instead of (known point subtracted from twice the mid-point).
entries.signal: Equals (mid-point) minus (known end point), coordinate by coordinate — the book's own answer equals 2×(mid-point) minus (known end point).

refutation.text_md: You set up the mid-point equation correctly and picked out the right numbers — the slip is in solving it: you treated $M=\frac{C+D}{2}$ as if it already said $M=C+D$, so the $\div2$ never got undone.
The book never skips that step. For $C(-2, 4)$ and $D(x, y)$ with mid-point $M(1, -3)$, its own working goes $1=\frac{-2+x}{2}$, then $1\times2=-2+x$, and only then $x=4$.

Skip the doubling and the same equation reads $1=-2+x$, giving $x=3$ — a different point from the book's answer $D(4, -10)$. The two routes disagree because $\div2$ changes the equation; it has to be cleared before you isolate the unknown coordinate, not ignored.

So whenever a mid-point coordinate sits alone on one side of $M=\frac{C+D}{2}$, multiply both sides by 2 first — that turns it into $2M=C+D$, which you can then rearrange to find the missing coordinate.

entries.label: Doubled the known point instead of the mid-point
entries.description: Mixes up which of the two given points is the mid-point, so doubles the known end point and subtracts the mid-point, instead of doubling the mid-point and subtracting the known end point.
entries.signal: Equals 2×(known end point) minus (mid-point), coordinate by coordinate — the book's own answer equals 2×(mid-point) minus (known end point).

refutation.text_md: You've got the right shape — double one point and subtract the other — but the point you doubled was the known end point, not the mid-point, so the two points swapped jobs.

In "$M(2, -2)$ is the mid-point of $AB$ with $A(3, 1)$", it's $M$ that sits halfway between $A$ and $B$, so it's $M$ that has to be doubled: $2\times(2, -2)-(3, 1)=(1, -5)$, the book's own answer for $B$.

Doubling $A$ instead and subtracting $M$ gives $2\times(3, 1)-(2, -2)=(4, 4)$ — a different point, because $M=\frac{A+B}{2}$ only balances as $2M=A+B$ when it's $M$ that's doubled; doubling $A$ builds a different equation altogether.

So before doubling anything, check which of the two given points the question actually calls the mid-point — that's the one you double, then subtract the other given point to reach the unknown end point.

entries.label: Pairing an adjacent vertex, not the opposite one, as the diagonal partner
entries.description: The student sets the mid-point of a side (two vertices adjacent in the parallelogram's name, such as $EF$ in $EFGH$) equal to the mid-point of the opposite side, instead of pairing the vertices that are two letters apart -- the true diagonals -- so they solve for the unknown vertex against the wrong known pair.
entries.signal: Recognisable by recomputing: if the submitted $(x, y)$ matches what you get from setting the mid-point of an adjacent-vertex segment (a side) equal to the mid-point of the segment through the unknown vertex and its other neighbour, rather than from the true diagonal pairing, this is the error -- there is no single fixed wrong value, since the pairing (and so the number) changes with each question's own labelled points.

refutation.text_md: You've paired the unknown vertex with a vertex next to it instead of the one actually opposite it. It's a fair guess: in a problem like $EFGH$ you already know $E$, $F$ and $G$, so it feels natural to pair the two points you already have into one segment ($EF$) and let the other pairing follow ($GH$, with the unknown vertex). You've correctly spotted that a parallelogram gives you two pairs of points whose mid-points must match -- you've just paired the wrong two.

But $EF$ and $GH$ are sides of $EFGH$, not diagonals. Walking round the shape in order, $E \to F \to G \to H \to E$, so $EF$, $FG$, $GH$ and $HE$ are the four sides. The diagonals are the two segments that skip a letter: $EG$ and $FH$. It's the diagonals that bisect each other in a parallelogram, not the sides.

Look what the wrong pairing does to the book's own worked example, where $E(-1, 0)$, $F(0, 3)$, $G(8, 11)$: the mid-point of $EF$ is $(-0.5, 1.5)$, and setting that equal to the mid-point of $GH$ gives $H(-9, -8)$ -- nowhere near the book's answer of $H(7, 8)$. The mismatch is exactly because $EF$ and $GH$ are sides, not diagonals, so their mid-points have no reason to be equal.

So before you reach for the mid-point formula, write out the parallelogram's name and check which letter is two places from the unknown one, skipping one letter in either direction -- that vertex is always its diagonal partner: in $EFGH$, $H$ pairs with $F$; in $PQRS$, $S$ pairs with $Q$. Find the mid-point of the diagonal whose two ends you already know, then use that same mid-point with the other diagonal's one known end to solve for the unknown vertex -- exactly the method the book uses every time.
